articles.title: Brain stimulation temporarily changes perception of sexualized images of women
articles.description: Applying mild electrical stimulation to the brain temporarily removed a perceptual bias linked to the sexual objectification of women, in the first study of its kind. The study is published in the journal Social Neuroscience.

articles.title: RNA archiving method reveals what a cell did days ago
articles.description: Information on what a cell did a few hours or days ago is generally unavailable to researchers, who can only measure the cell's current status. This is a problem if the aim is to understand how immune responses arise or why individual cancer cells survive treatment.

articles.title: Thousands of students across Oregon celebrate National Farm to School month
articles.description: More than 40,000 students in almost 100 Oregon school districts participated in the "Oregon Crunch at Once" event celebrating Farm to School month.

articles.title: Diamond defects confirm 80-year-old theory of crystal stress
articles.description: For the first time, researchers in Japan have directly mapped several components of the stress field surrounding an atomic-scale flaw in the crystal structure of diamond. Led by Tokuyuki Teraji at Japan's National Institute for Materials Science, the team achieved its result using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, whose spin states respond differently to stress depending on how they are oriented relative to the stress field.

articles.title: Tiny shifts in iron content tip a potential memory material between competing magnetic states
articles.description: A team of Yale researchers has figured out what gives a magnetic material its mysterious properties, a discovery that could help boost computing memory and the field of "spintronics." Their work is published in Physical Review Letters.

articles.title: Thermal priming enhances heat tolerance and yield in tomatoes after recurrent heat stress
articles.description: High temperatures can significantly impair the growth and yield of crops, including tomatoes. A new study by an international research team led by Dr. Justyna Olas, of the Leibniz Institute for Horticultural Sciences (IGZ), has shown that tomatoes can respond better to subsequent heat stress following moderate heat exposure. The work is published in The Plant Journal.

articles.title: An 'electron waiting room' helps blue titanium dioxide hold light energy longer
articles.description: To produce hydrogen using sunlight, the energy obtained from light must be retained until it can be used in a chemical reaction. However, if an electron that has gained energy from light quickly returns to its original position, it becomes difficult to make use of that energy.

articles.title: Q&A: When it comes to democratic backsliding, our federalist system is a two-way street
articles.description: As the 2026 midterm elections approach, the signs of democratic backsliding are everywhere across the U.S. political landscape. Troubling signs include the Trump administration's demand for state voter roll data and interference with mail-in voting, the pressure it applied to Georgia election officials to reverse Joe Biden's victory in that state in the 2020 election and, of course, extreme partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts.

articles.description: Nobel Physics prize winner Geoffrey Hinton is widely regarded as one of the godfathers of artificial intelligence, but he's spent much of the last few years warning against its potential dangers. He discussed those ideas at Starmus and also revealed why 'The Terminator' is his favourite film.

articles.title: FAST and Arecibo point to possible dark galaxy with vast hydrogen reservoir
articles.description: Astronomers have found a vast reservoir of hydrogen with something conspicuously missing: detectable starlight. The object, called AGC 322753, contains roughly 2 billion times the sun's mass in neutral hydrogen, a potential supply of material for making stars. Its radio signal suggests the gas may be rotating in a disk, yet deep astronomical images reveal no matching glow.

articles.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
articles.description: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

articles.title: UC Berkeley’s new AI-research building is designed for human interaction
articles.description: At UC Berkeley’s new College of Computing, Data Science, and Society, an interlocking building of curved glass and sleek columns, the building has been designed so that the technologies of the future inevitably collide. The 367,000-square-foot building, named the Barbara and Gerson Bakar Gateway, was designed by the architecture firm Weiss/Manfredi in collaboration with Gensler. It has lecture halls, labs, offices, and common areas for students and professors across a wide range of fields, including computer programming, robotics, and AI. The college’s inaugural dean, Jennifer Chayes, says the lines between academic fields are becoming so blurry it makes sense to bring all these different courses of study under one roof and literally remove many of the walls that would have otherwise separated them. “The building is porous in a way that other buildings are not, reflecting the disciplinary porosity of the college, and the fact that we want all of our students to emerge with an ethos of compassion and a deep sense of responsibility to society,” Chayes says. Chayes, who spent 23 years at Microsoft as a technical fellow and lab director, came to the University of California, Berkeley, in 2020 to build the institution’s first new college in more than 50 years. And she wanted a building that would live up to the college’s mission and potential. Working closely with the architects Marion Weiss and Michael Manfredi throughout the design process, she was not shy about pursuing that vision. “I wrote them poetry and prose about how I hoped the building would make people feel,” Chayes says. “And I think I rejected their first four designs. So the architects might have considered me the client from hell.” That wasn’t the case. Weiss and Manfredi embraced Chayes’s concept for the building, putting an atypical emphasis on common areas, which make up the majority of the building’s square footage, and dedicating less space than usual to private offices and classrooms. “That, I think, is one of the most significant aspects of the project, which is a very high degree of public space, and space that is unprogrammed,” says Manfredi. “And the reason for that is that Jennifer knows that no matter what kinds of programs she and her faculty will be developing this year, in five years there’ll be a different set of programs.” Teaching a rapidly evolving topic like artificial intelligence is one challenge, but designing for the decades-long life of such a college building required some deeper thinking about what would stand the test of time. Chayes, a mathematician by training, thought of one constant: food. “Certain fields were launched from the social kitchens of our Microsoft research labs,” she says. “I felt it was really important that we bring people together.” Each of the building’s five floors has two social kitchens, café-like pantries where people can grab a coffee, heat up lunch, or have an informal meeting. Hao Ko, global director of design at Gensler, which led the workplace design element of the project, calls the social kitchen “a magnified experience” of the coffee stations within conventional academic buildings. “You can have a meeting for a whole department in the social kitchen because we can expand that space,” he says. “People like to work in a café environment, so we also have work areas, and there are whiteboards everywhere.” The social kitchens are intentionally tucked into parts of each floor that are away from most offices, labs, and classrooms, as are bathrooms and elevators. It’s another way of encouraging movement and interaction. “These are landmarks and destinations that get people moving through the building,” says Sandy Mendler, an education leader at Gensler. The overall form of the building was shaped by the way people would move through it. Chayes often talked with the architects about creating piazza-like areas of openness that people would cross on their way to a lab space or a social kitchen. So Weiss/Manfredi designed a large central piazza in the form of an atrium surrounded by curving staircases and topped with a skylight. Long sightlines around its edges make the atrium act as a place where people can see and run into each other. “It becomes the primary way of moving up and down,” Weiss says. “So again, every opportunity to kind of provide high levels of connection between floors or across floors was prioritized both academically by Jennifer’s team but also architecturally.” The atrium also becomes a source of natural light, along with two scoop-like spaces cutting into the building’s volume. Manfredi says people inside are never more than 30 feet away from a window. Since the building’s opening a few months ago, it’s already become a hive of activity, much more so than buildings dominated by classrooms and private offices. People call out to each other across the atrium or meet for quick chats on its spiraling stairs, Chayes says. But it’s not all serendipity and togetherness. Chayes says the atrium has also become a space where people just gravitate alone and dwell. “I just find people kind of lost in thought, gazing out at the atrium,” she says. “I didn’t think of it this way when they designed it, but it almost has a cathedral feel to it.” Having that space to think could be just as important as having the room to share ideas with others.

articles.title: The Social Reckoning: an untethered companion piece
articles.description: As a fan of The Social Network, I was thrilled to hear there was a sequel in the works. David Fincher's 2010 film about Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook's origins was a brilliant, fast-paced drama. It had an award-winning score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross (names you may recognize from the Challengers soundtrack) and incredibly strong acting from Jesse Eisenberg, Andrew Garfield and others. Unfortunately, its sequel, The Social Reckoning, is unable to reach even a fraction of the original's greatness. The Social Reckoning follows Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a Facebook engineer who uncovers internal data proving Facebook's algorithm actively radicalizes and harms users, and Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), an investigative journalist from the Wall Street Journal hellbent on publishing Haugen's story. The film's plot ultimately revolves around Haugen's decision to go public with the information and seek whistleblower status in court. The teams behind the two movies had very little overlap. Fincher's directing was key to making The Social Network as great as it was, but he didn't return to direct the sequel. Instead, Aaron Sorkin, who wrote the original screenplay for The Social Network, directed, produced and wrote this movie as his fourth-ever directing job. Unfortunately, he is unable to recreate Fincher's magic. Fincher's minimalist style emphasized subtext and complexity, and unfortunately this sequel could not stray further from that "show don't tell" ethos. To point out some of the specific problems I had with the movie, I want to start with the key issue: why was this movie made? What is it trying to tell us? A movie is only interesting if it is presenting the audience with new information or presenting old information in a new and innovative way. The Social Network presented a story that many people already partially knew, but presented it in a very captivating and cinematic way. Though many knew the basic facts about Zuckerberg's creation of Facebook at Harvard, the dramatic twists and turns with co-creator Eduardo Saverin and the legal battle with the Winklevoss twins and the looming trial added drama and excitement to the plot. That dramatization allowed the film to dive deeper into what Facebook was below the surface through the dramatic and new retelling. The Social Dilemma, however, presents old information in an uninteresting way. Most of us were around for the Facebook trial in 2021. We remember the outcome and the information shared. It was revealed that Facebook amplified anger and division and didn't moderate their content responsibly; however they got away with it more or less scot-free. $17 billion is a drop in the bucket for an almost $2 trillion dollar company. Even if we don't remember the trial specifically, many are social media-literate enough to understand that the algorithm seeks engagement at all costs. This movie is presenting that information to the audience as if it is a shocking revelation, a message that falls flat in 2026. Beyond the generally lackluster concept of the film, the characters are deeply unrealistic and unrelatable. I found Madison's characterization of Haugen bland at best and annoying at worst. Haugen is presented as an "adorkable" nerd with a heart of gold, but honestly there was nothing that interesting about the character. It felt like a caricature I'd already seen in dozens of other films. White's portrayal of Horwitz is slightly better, but not by much. Horwitz is essentially the same character as Haugen, except with less technological smarts. I wish that were an exaggeration, but they are genuinely presented with the exact same character traits. They both boil down to being deeply good individuals who struggle but ultimately want to do the right thing. Watching two genuinely moral people succeed can be satisfying, but this film fails to get me to actually root for the protagonists enough to enjoy watching them. Additionally, the sheer blandness of these characters leads to a circular plot. The movie is essentially two hours of Haugen slowly agreeing to help Horwitz, then saying she won't help him anymore and then deciding to help him again. This cycle repeats five or six times throughout the movie, and it becomes deeply uninteresting especially given the commonly held prior knowledge that she did decide to become a whistleblower. Finally, I would remiss if I did not point out the breathtakingly cliché dialogue in this movie. At the climax of the film, when Haugen finally decides (for what seems like the hundredth time) to abandon her work with Horwitz, she makes a trite speech about how "art and film made being a hero seem so easy." She references "heroes" like John Proctor and the main character in A Tale of Two Cities whose name she forgot before finally ending with "Even Gandalf, goddamn it!" Needless to say, this speech fell on deaf ears for me. Never once in this movie did I sincerely feel Haugen struggle with the life-altering decisions she was making, and this speech did nothing to help that impression. Unfortunately, this speech is only one thread in the tapestry of this movie's lackluster, cheesy dialogue. There were myriad attempts at humor that fell quite flat, including a lot of unsubtle references to The Social Network. It was clearly just what Sorkin found funny, but that didn't resonate with me or seemingly anyone else in the audience. Above all else, The Social Reckoning was simply a boring film that had little to say. I would not recommend watching this movie, especially if you are looking for a companion piece to The Social Network. While there are a few highlights, such as Strong's great performance as Zuckerberg or the moments of interest that Horwitz's interns bring to the film, it is a bland and uninteresting movie.
